title: Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a dependable interface through which signed-language and spoken-language users could hold live, two-way conversations. It would interpret signed input into speech or text and spoken input into understandable signed output while preserving meaning, expression, context, and conversational intent. Its defining contribution would be the complete interaction: participants could take turns naturally, recognize uncertainty, correct misunderstandings, and pause or stop translation. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement demonstrated by the supplied papers.

Signed communication cannot be understood by treating signs as word-for-word substitutes for spoken language. The supplied FLEURS-ASL review documents grammatical facial expression, meaningful facial and body language, regional and stylistic variation, and comprehension that depends on surrounding context. The evidence is principally about ASL; it should not be treated as an exhaustive comparative account of all signed languages. Nevertheless, it explains why an interface must capture more than hand movements and why translating isolated, prepared clips is an incomplete test of conversational understanding.

The relevant research addresses different parts of this proposed system. FLEURS-ASL evaluates understanding primarily through ASL-to-English-text tasks, while SignLLM investigates multilingual text- or prompt-to-pose production. Connecting recognition, translation, speech processing, and sign generation would be an engineering starting point. As an integration judgment, successful conversation would still require separate evidence that these components work together with usable timing, intelligible output, repair, and participant control.

significance.text: If demonstrated dependably, this interface could allow signed-language and spoken-language users to communicate directly in more everyday situations when a qualified interpreter is unavailable. SignLLM identifies communication between Deaf people and family members without sign-language knowledge as an application goal, while acknowledging that its current accuracy is insufficient for full trust. The proposed benefit therefore depends on overcoming reliability limitations, rather than following automatically from the existence of a sign-generation model.

As a conditional impact assessment, the revolutionary change would be making communication available as an ongoing, controllable conversation instead of a sequence of disconnected translation requests. Participants could clarify references, repair mistakes, and respond to one another as the exchange develops. Broader participation in family life, services, education, or work would be plausible downstream possibilities, but would depend on the language coverage, affordability, acceptance, and deployment conditions actually demonstrated.

The analogy to ordinary machine translation has important limits. A convincing result would need to preserve visually expressed grammar and context, and generated movement would need to be understandable to its intended users. Neither successful text translation nor favorable automated production metrics alone establishes that capability. Universal language coverage, interpreter-equivalent performance, or reliable operation in every consequential setting would require evidence beyond the supplied component studies; the proposed innovation makes none of those guarantees.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this proposal is dependable, live, bidirectional interpretation integrated into a usable conversation. The supplied studies leave a substantial gap between prepared input or generated pose sequences and spontaneous dialogue. FLEURS-ASL documents restrictions in signer and dialect coverage, recording environments, and spontaneous language, while its evaluated understanding models remained substantially below human performance. These findings identify barriers for the evaluated systems and benchmark; they do not establish the limits of every system in the field.

On the input side, the interface would need to interpret hand movements together with facial and body expression and the context accumulated across an exchange. Regional and stylistic variation make coverage a substantive language problem, not simply a matter of recognizing a larger list of signs. The difficulty of evaluating isolated sentences also creates a measurement barrier: a system can perform well on selected clips without establishing that it tracks meaning across a live conversation.

On the output side, producing a pose sequence is only part of producing understandable signed language. SignLLM's reviewed limitations include accuracy, rendering, and processing issues, including manual processing that prevents a fully end-to-end pipeline. Its chiefly automated back-translation evaluation does not by itself establish participant intelligibility, expressive adequacy, or readiness for conversation. A practical interface would have to close those gaps while sustaining the timing needed for an exchange.

As proposed interaction requirements, uncertainty handling, repair, consent, and user agency are additional engineering challenges. The interface must make uncertainty visible without overwhelming the conversation, give participants a way to correct meaning, and support transparent escalation when communication cannot proceed reliably. These are design obligations inferred from the intended use, not capabilities established by the papers or published consensus completion standards.

current_state.text: Garrett Tanzer's “FLEURS-ASL: Including American Sign Language in Massively Multilingual Multitask Evaluation,” published at NAACL in 2025, introduces an evaluation resource translated by five Certified Deaf Interpreters and reports ASL-to-English-text baselines. The reviewed paper reports a substantial gap between the evaluated models and human performance. Its contribution is a benchmark and component evaluation, not a demonstration of live, bidirectional interpretation.

FLEURS-ASL uses prepared monologues rather than dialogues. Its limited signer and dialect coverage, professional recording environments, and restricted coverage of spontaneously produced language constrain what can be concluded about everyday interaction. These limitations do not negate the benchmark's value; they mean that its results cannot establish performance in consenting participants' spontaneous two-way conversations.

Sen Fang, Chen Chen, Lei Wang, Ce Zheng, Chunyu Sui, and Yapeng Tian's “SignLLM: Sign Language Production Large Language Models,” published in the ICCV Workshops in 2025, investigates multilingual text- and prompt-to-pose production. The supplied review describes evaluation chiefly through automated back-translation metrics and reports remaining accuracy, rendering, and processing limitations. The authors acknowledge insufficient accuracy for full trust and a pipeline that is not fully end-to-end. This supports progress on sign production, without establishing that generated output is sufficient for live conversations.

The earlier research account reported an access error for SignLLM. The supplied review subsequently assessed saved, complete extracted text for both papers, with no declared truncation or extraction issues, so that earlier access problem no longer prevents reporting the reviewed textual findings. The review did not inspect figure images for these judgments; no conclusion about visual rendering quality is inferred from those uninspected images.

Taken together, the supplied 2025 papers document relevant components but do not demonstrate the complete proposed conversational interface. The supplied freshness record is empty, leaving field-wide status as of November 1, 2026 unresolved. These dated findings therefore support a bounded account of the two studies, not a claim that no complete interface had been demonstrated elsewhere by that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: consenting Deaf and hearing participants would use the interface for live, unscripted, two-way conversations across explicitly selected signed and spoken language pairs, dialects, participants, and settings. Testing would assess both directions of communication and the exchange as a whole. This would address the conversational scope missing from prepared monologues and isolated production evaluations, but would establish demonstrated breadth only within the tested conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Live unscripted two-way conversations across selected signed–spoken language pairs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assessment: independent qualified interpreters would evaluate preservation of meaning, pragmatic intent, and consequential errors, while participants would evaluate intelligibility, timing, and control. Evaluation should distinguish understandable signed output from a pose sequence that receives a favorable automated score. These complementary assessments follow from the limitations of the supplied understanding and production evaluations; the papers do not prescribe this exact protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Interpreter and participant evaluations assess meaning preservation and usability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol requirements: specify language and dialect coverage, participant recruitment, latency and error thresholds, and uncertainty handling before evaluation. Include misunderstandings that require repair and verify that participants can correct, pause, or stop translation and recognize when escalation is needed. No numerical pass thresholds are established by the supplied evidence; suitable thresholds would need justification for the intended setting and consequences of error.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified evaluation criteria verify conversational repair and participant control

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should be able to repeat the evaluation with documented system versions, operating conditions, and consent-compatible materials or procedures. Results should report failures and variation across participants, language pairs, dialects, and settings, alongside any human assistance or manual processing. Success should be described within those boundaries. Finite tests cannot establish literal universality, and performance suitable for one everyday setting would not automatically establish suitability for a more consequential one.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication and reported limitations establish demonstrated practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user's chosen modality,” shares the goal of removing modality barriers. HCI-08 specifically concerns communication between people across languages, including conversational meaning and timing; HCI-04 concerns operating software. HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” also concerns communication access, but its defining challenge is enabling communication and control after profound paralysis rather than interpretation between signed and spoken languages.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” overlaps with HCI-08 in expression, turn-taking, and shared context. Preserving social cues during collaboration does not itself translate between languages, while accurate translation alone does not establish usable remote collaboration. HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” and HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” concern other interface capabilities; display or haptic fidelity does not establish linguistic accuracy or conversational effectiveness.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” shares the concern for correction, uncertainty, and meaningful user control. In HCI-08 those requirements apply to mediation of a conversation rather than delegation of computer work. HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” is relevant to control over conversational information, while HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” concerns retained personal information. Neither privacy management nor durable memory is the defining breakthrough of HCI-08.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could inform explanations and predictions of conversational usability, but is a broader scientific ambition rather than this particular interface. HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” shares concerns about comprehensibility and correction while addressing the creation and maintenance of programs. HCI-08 remains a distinct innovation whose technical overlap with machine translation, computer vision, sign linguistics, speech technology, avatar generation, and accessibility serves a specific conversational goal.

change_log.reason: The research and review identify the complete conversational interaction as the innovation; translation and production models are components.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad claim that the complete interface remains unproven with a conclusion bounded to the supplied papers.
change_log.reason: Two studies and an empty freshness record cannot establish field-wide absence as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Replaced the SignLLM access-error caveat with the supplied review's findings from complete saved text, while retaining the limitation on uninspected images.
change_log.reason: The later review could assess textual limitations, but did not establish visual quality through figure inspection.

change_log.change: Added FLEURS-ASL's prepared-monologue scope, limited coverage and recording conditions, and reported model–human performance gap.
change_log.reason: These details explain both the benchmark's contribution and why its results do not establish spontaneous conversational performance.

change_log.change: Specified SignLLM's text/prompt-to-pose scope, chiefly automated back-translation evaluation, and reported accuracy, rendering, and processing limitations.
change_log.reason: These distinctions prevent pose generation or automated scores from being presented as demonstrated participant intelligibility or conversational readiness.

change_log.change: Qualified the linguistic generalization and conditional impact claims.
change_log.reason: The detailed linguistic evidence is principally about ASL, and the supplied studies do not establish universal coverage, interpreter equivalence, or dependable use in every consequential setting.

change_log.change: Developed proposed completion criteria covering live dialogue, complementary human assessments, repair, reproducibility, and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original proposal was coherent but needed clearer separation between suggested evaluation requirements and established standards.

change_log.change: Added distinct roster relationships and separated direct communication benefits from conditional downstream possibilities.
change_log.reason: This preserves the concept's scope without merging adjacent innovations or treating anticipated impact as a demonstrated result.

unresolved_issues: Field-wide progress as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The supplied evidence does not establish which language pairs, dialects, participants, or everyday settings a complete interface could reliably support.
An executable evaluation still requires justified latency and error thresholds, recruitment plans, uncertainty procedures, and setting-specific acceptance criteria.
Participant intelligibility and conversational effectiveness of SignLLM outputs are not established by the reviewed automated evaluation; visual quality was not independently assessed from figures.
The practical extent of human assistance or manual processing in an integrated conversational system remains to be demonstrated.

brief.title: Live conversations between people who sign and speak
possible: A Deaf person could talk with a family member who does not sign, with signing translated into speech or text and speech translated into understandable signing. Both people could take turns naturally, clarify meaning, correct mistakes, and pause or stop translation.
why: This could make direct communication available in more everyday situations when a qualified interpreter is unavailable. Conversations could keep their context as people respond to each other, supporting participation in family life, services, education, and work.

sources.showed: Tanzer built FLEURS-ASL, a translation test using American Sign Language prepared by Certified Deaf Interpreters. His model matched or exceeded earlier models on translating signing into English text.
sources.quote:
This model
meets or exceeds the performance of phrase-
level baselines while supporting a multitude
of new tasks.
sources.cited_for: The study tests understanding of signed language and reports a substantial gap between model and human performance.
sources.not_established: Prepared monologues do not establish dependable understanding during spontaneous conversations.

sources.who: Sen Fang, Chen Chen, Lei Wang, Ce Zheng, Chunyu Sui and Yapeng Tian
sources.showed: The team built SignLLM to turn text or written requests into pose sequences, digital descriptions of body movements, across eight signed languages. It outperformed comparison models on automated tests.
sources.quote:
It can pro-
duce the sign language representation of eight languages
from texts or prompts.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates a component for generating signed output from written input.
sources.not_established: Automated scores do not establish that people can understand the generated signing well enough for live conversation.

shown: Tanzer and the SignLLM team have demonstrated separate parts of the task: interpreting signed input and generating signed output. Neither study demonstrates a complete live conversation system. SignLLM still has accuracy limitations and requires manual processing.
missing: A complete system would need to preserve meaning through spontaneous exchanges, including facial grammar, body expression, and conversational context.
Generated signing would need to remain understandable and expressive at a pace that supports natural turn-taking.
Participants would need usable ways to recognize uncertainty, repair misunderstandings, and control translation.

milestones.label: Live, unscripted conversations work in both directions
milestones.explanation: Consenting Deaf and hearing participants would have to converse spontaneously across specified language pairs, dialects, and settings. This would establish performance across a whole exchange within those conditions.

milestones.label: Interpreters and participants confirm meaning and usability
milestones.explanation: Independent qualified interpreters would have to assess meaning, intent, and serious errors, while participants assess understanding, timing, and control. This would test whether translation actually serves the conversation.

milestones.label: Defined tests confirm repair and participant control
milestones.explanation: Tests with criteria set beforehand would have to cover language coverage, recruitment, delays, errors, uncertainty, correction, pausing, stopping, and escalation. This would establish how participants can manage failures.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat tests under documented conditions, reporting failures, variation, and human assistance through consent-compatible procedures. This would establish reproducibility and practical boundaries.

uncertain: Which language pairs, dialects, participants, and everyday settings could a complete system reliably support?
Acceptable delays and error rates still need justification for the setting and the consequences of mistakes.
How much human assistance or manual processing would an integrated conversation system require?

page.title: Real-time bidirectional signed–spoken language translation
page.definition: Two people take turns on one mobile device. One signs on camera and the other receives speech or text. A spoken or typed reply appears as signing by an animated figure. SignON specified messages of up to 30 seconds and a two-second translation-response target across five signed and four spoken languages. Its version 3 prototype supported signing in the Sign Language of the Netherlands.

goal.need: About one million deaf people in the EU used a sign language in 2016. Without an interpreter, signers may rely on lipreading, speech or writing. A parent who signs could ask a Dutch-speaking childcare worker about their child’s day in Flemish Sign Language and receive the answer in the same language. Captions alone cover only the worker’s side of that exchange. The signed reply must preserve meaning in context. Qualified interpreters remain essential where the exchange calls for their judgment.

completion.title: A mobile translator meets SignON’s TRL 7, response-time and user-acceptance targets.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate the system prototype in an operational environment (technology readiness level 7) on standard modern mobile devices without additional special equipment. Translate in both directions between each of the five signed languages and English, Irish, Dutch and Spanish speech or text. For these exchanges, D1.6 Annex A specifies conversion within two seconds. Its five-second exception is for sign-to-sign translation. Section 2 separately summarises response time as two to five seconds. Translation accuracy must be acceptable to 75% of users, and average satisfaction with the overall service must reach at least 75%.
completion.set_by: EU-funded SignON consortium, D7.4 Section 6, Objectives 1 and 2, and D1.6 Section 2 and Annex A. The quoted device and readiness requirement is in the Objective 2 success-measures table.
completion.threshold_quote: Application and Service at TRL 7 running on standard modern mobile devices without the need for additional special equipment.
completion.basis: SignON assessed its prototype at level 6. Version 3 supported signing in the Sign Language of the Netherlands. Of 68 invited users, 22 responded, including six sign-language users. The overall ratings were 55% for the usefulness of translation accuracy and 60% for satisfaction with the service. Both are questionnaire scores. The targets are specific to SignON and provide no certification of interpreter equivalence or unscripted dialogue.

milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an experimental exchange for the signed language under assessment. Translate a signed video message into speech or text and a spoken or typed message into signing.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G; generic maturity definition, not a sign-language-specific performance threshold.

milestones.title: Signed–spoken translation technology is validated in the laboratory (TRL 4).
milestones.criterion: Validate both translation directions in the laboratory for the signed language under assessment, from signed video to speech or text and from speech or text to signing.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G; generic maturity definition used in SignON’s readiness framework.

milestones.title: A signed–spoken mobile translator is demonstrated in a relevant environment (TRL 6).
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the integrated mobile prototype translating in both directions for the signed language under assessment in an environment relevant to its intended face-to-face use.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G; SignON applies this definition in D7.4, Task 2.3.

milestones.title: A signed–spoken translation app achieves a System Usability Scale score of at least 68.
milestones.criterion: After participants use the integrated translation app, administer the ten-item System Usability Scale. The mean participant score must reach at least 68.0 on the 0–100 scale.
milestones.set_by: SignON consortium, D1.6, Section 2.2, adopting a System Usability Scale acceptance threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: A SUS Rating of 68.0 is the threshold to indicate acceptable usability,

milestones.title: A two-way signed–spoken translator is validated in a relevant environment (TRL 5).
milestones.criterion: Validate both translation directions for the signed language under assessment in an environment relevant to the intended face-to-face exchange.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, Horizon 2020 General Annex G, technology readiness level 5.

not_found: No sign-language-specific pass criteria for TRL 3–6 were found; the milestones use the Commission’s maturity definitions applied by SignON.
No separate integrated-system validation or user-acceptance outcome for each tracked signed language was found in the opened SignON reports.
No reconciliation of SignON’s 2-second and 2–5-second response targets, or precise timing boundaries for them, was found.
No consensus completion test for unscripted bidirectional dialogue, conversational repair or interpreter equivalence was found in the programme, standards and professional-body searches.
The supplied SignLLM conference PDF returned HTTP 403; its arXiv version revised on 30 April 2025 was opened instead.
The ISO/IEC DIS 20071-24 preview exposed only a JavaScript shell, so its requirements could not be inspected.

definition = "Two people take turns on one mobile device. One signs on camera and the other receives speech or text. A spoken or typed reply appears as signing by an animated figure. SignON specified messages of up to 30 seconds and a two-second translation-response target across five signed and four spoken languages. Its version 3 prototype supported signing in the Sign Language of the Netherlands.". Reason: The 30-second message limit clarifies what real time means here, and the release report distinguishes the five-language target from the prototype’s actual coverage.

goal.need = "About one million deaf people in the EU used a sign language in 2016. Without an interpreter, signers may rely on lipreading, speech or writing. A parent who signs could ask a Dutch-speaking childcare worker about their child\u2019s day in Flemish Sign Language and receive the answer in the same language. Captions alone cover only the worker\u2019s side of that exchange. The signed reply must preserve meaning in context. Qualified interpreters remain essential where the exchange calls for their judgment.". Reason: The current paragraph reports prototype scores where readers need the scale of the communication barrier and an example of what two-way translation would let people do.

add statement by European Commission, Horizon 2020 topic ICT-57-2020, 2020: "Develop novel mobile applications translating between speech and sign languages". Reason: The Commission’s funding call names the mobile translation goal more precisely than either project’s general statement about communication.

add statement by World Federation of the Deaf and World Association of Sign Language Interpreters, 2018: "caution against the use of signing avatars as a replacement for human signers.". Reason: The joint statement supplies the position of deaf and interpreter organisations on using avatars in place of human signers.

edit completion: criterion = "Demonstrate the system prototype in an operational environment (technology readiness level 7) on standard modern mobile devices without additional special equipment. Translate in both directions between each of the five signed languages and English, Irish, Dutch and Spanish speech or text. For these exchanges, D1.6 Annex A specifies conversion within two seconds. Its five-second exception is for sign-to-sign translation. Section 2 separately summarises response time as two to five seconds. Translation accuracy must be acceptable to 75% of users, and average satisfaction with the overall service must reach at least 75%."; set_by = "EU-funded SignON consortium, D7.4 Section 6, Objectives 1 and 2, and D1.6 Section 2 and Annex A. The quoted device and readiness requirement is in the Objective 2 success-measures table."; threshold_quote = "Application and Service at TRL 7 running on standard modern mobile devices without the need for additional special equipment."; threshold_ref = 4; basis = "SignON assessed its prototype at level 6. Version 3 supported signing in the Sign Language of the Netherlands. Of 68 invited users, 22 responded, including six sign-language users. The overall ratings were 55% for the usefulness of translation accuracy and 60% for satisfaction with the service. Both are questionnaire scores. The targets are specific to SignON and provide no certification of interpreter equivalence or unscripted dialogue."; refs = [4, 5, 2, 1, 13]. Reason: The final report places the success measures in Section 6, and the assessment distinguishes the sign-to-sign timing exception and users’ ratings from measured translation accuracy.

edit m1: title = "A signed\u2013spoken translator demonstrates both directions in an experimental proof of concept (TRL 3)."; criterion = "Demonstrate an experimental exchange for the signed language under assessment. Translate a signed video message into speech or text and a spoken or typed message into signing."; threshold_quote = "experimental proof of concept"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 1, 20]. Reason: The criterion currently includes one-way American Sign Language results that cannot establish an experimental two-way exchange for a tracked language.

edit m2: criterion = "Validate both translation directions in the laboratory for the signed language under assessment, from signed video to speech or text and from speech or text to signing."; threshold_quote = "technology validated in lab"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 1]. Reason: The existing criterion mixes laboratory validation with an inventory of recognition models and fingerspelling features.

add milestone after m2: "A two-way signed–spoken translator is validated in a relevant environment (TRL 5).". Reason: The sequence skips the Commission’s level 5 distinction between validation in the laboratory and demonstration in a relevant environment.

edit m3: criterion = "Demonstrate the integrated mobile prototype translating in both directions for the signed language under assessment in an environment relevant to its intended face-to-face use."; threshold_quote = "technology demonstrated in relevant environment"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 4, 1]. Reason: The criterion currently includes the consortium’s readiness verdict without specifying what a demonstration must show for an individual signed language.

edit m4: criterion = "After participants use the integrated translation app, administer the ten-item System Usability Scale. The mean participant score must reach at least 68.0 on the 0\u2013100 scale."; threshold_quote = "A SUS Rating of 68.0 is the threshold to indicate acceptable usability,"; threshold_ref = 2; refs = [2]. Reason: The revised criterion identifies the questionnaire, scale and group average while removing the observed scores from the pass condition.
